title: Calculating Centers of Mass and Moments of Inertia
short: Calculating Centers of Mass and Moments of Inertia
lead: A flat plate or a solid of varying density has a mass, moments and a balance point, each an integral of its density. This section finds the mass, moments, center of mass and moments of inertia of a lamina by double integrals and of a solid by triple integrals.
objectives: Use double integrals to locate the center of mass of a two-dimensional object.
Use double integrals to find the moment of inertia of a two-dimensional object.
Use triple integrals to locate the center of mass of a three-dimensional object.
summary_html:
• For a lamina $\kR$ with a density function $\krho (x,y)$ at any point $(x,y)$ in the plane, the mass is $\km=\iint\limits_{\kR}\krho (x,y)dA .$
  • The moments about the $x\text{-axis}$ and $y\text{-axis}$ are $$\kMx=\iint\limits_{\kR}y\rho (x,y) dA\;\text{and}\;\kMy=\iint\limits_{\kR}x\rho (x,y) dA.$$
  • The center of mass is given by $\kxbar=\frac{\kMy}{\km},\kybar=\frac{\kMx}{\km}.$
  • The center of mass becomes the centroid of the plane when the density is constant.
  • The moments of inertia about the $x-\text{axis,}$ $y-\text{axis,}$ and the origin are $$\kIx=\iint\limits_{\kR}y^{2}\krho (x,y)dA, \; \;\kIy=\iint\limits_{\kR}x^{2}\krho (x,y)dA, \;\text{and}\;\kIzero=\kIx+\kIy=\iint\limits_{\kR}(x^{2}+y^{2})\krho (x,y)dA.$$ Finding the mass, center of mass, moments, and moments of inertia in triple integrals:
  • For a solid object $\kQ$ with a density function $\krho (x,y,z)$ at any point $(x,y,z)$ in space, the mass is $\km=\iiint\limits_{\kQ}\krho (x,y,z)dV .$
  • The moments about the $xy\text{-plane,}$ the $xz\text{-plane,}$ and the $yz\text{-plane}$ are $$\kMxy=\iiint\limits_{\kQ}z\rho (x,y,z)dV ,\;\kMxz=\iiint\limits_{\kQ}y\rho (x,y,z)dV ,\;\kMyz=\iiint\limits_{\kQ}x\rho (x,y,z)dV .$$
  • The center of mass is given by $\kxbar=\frac{\kMyz}{\km},\kybar=\frac{\kMxz}{\km},\kzbar=\frac{\kMxy}{\km}.$
  • The center of mass becomes the centroid of the solid when the density is constant.
  • The moments of inertia about the $yz\text{-plane,}$ the $xz\text{-plane,}$ and the $xy\text{-plane}$ are $$\begin{array}{l} \\ \kIx=\iiint\limits_{\kQ}(y^{2}+z^{2})\krho (x,y,z)dV, \kIy=\iiint\limits_{\kQ}(x^{2}+z^{2})\krho (x,y,z)dV, \\ \kIz=\iiint\limits_{\kQ}(x^{2}+y^{2})\krho (x,y,z)dV. \end{array}$$

The solid $Q$ of constant density $1$ is situated inside the sphere $x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=16$ and outside the sphere $x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=1.$ Show that the center of mass of the solid is not located within the solid.

answer.solution: The solid is the shell $1\le\rho\le 4$ of constant density, symmetric under each of the reflections $x\to -x,$ $y\to -y$ and $z\to -z.$ Each moment integrates an odd function over a symmetric region, so $M_{yz}=\iiint_{Q}x\,dV=0,$ and likewise $M_{xz}=M_{xy}=0;$ the mass is positive, so the center of mass is $(\bar{x},\bar{y},\bar{z})=(0,0,0).$ The origin is inside the inner sphere $x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=1,$ which is not part of $Q,$ so the center of mass is not located within the solid.

The solid $Q$ is bounded by the planes $x+y+z=3,$ $x=0,y=0,$ and $z=0.$ Its density is $\rho (x,y,z)=x+ay,$ where $a\gt 0.$ Show that the center of mass of the solid is located in the plane $z=\frac{3}{5}$ for any value of $a.$

answer.solution: On the tetrahedron $x+y+z\le 3$ in the first octant the variables $x$ and $y$ play the same part, so $\iiint_{Q}y\,dV=\iiint_{Q}x\,dV$ and $\iiint_{Q}yz\,dV=\iiint_{Q}xz\,dV.$ Hence $m=\iiint_{Q}(x+ay)\,dV=(1+a)\iiint_{Q}x\,dV$ and $M_{xy}=\iiint_{Q}z(x+ay)\,dV=(1+a)\iiint_{Q}xz\,dV.$ Computing, $\iiint_{Q}x\,dV=\int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{3-x}\int_{0}^{3-x-y}x\,dz\,dy\,dx=\frac{27}{8}$ and $\iiint_{Q}xz\,dV=\frac{81}{40},$ so $\bar{z}=\frac{M_{xy}}{m}=\frac{81/40}{27/8}=\frac{3}{5},$ whatever the value of $a.$

The solid $Q=\{(x,y,z)|0\le x^{2}+y^{2}\le 16,x\ge 0,y\ge 0,0\le z\le x\}$ has the density $\rho (x,y,z)=k.$ Show that the moment $M_{xy}$ about the $xy\text{-plane}$ is half of the moment $M_{yz}$ about the $yz\text{-plane}\text{.}$

answer.solution: With constant density $k,$ $M_{xy}=k\iiint_{Q}z\,dV=k\iint_{D}\int_{0}^{x}z\,dz\,dA=\frac{k}{2}\iint_{D}x^{2}\,dA$ and $M_{yz}=k\iiint_{Q}x\,dV=k\iint_{D}\int_{0}^{x}x\,dz\,dA=k\iint_{D}x^{2}\,dA,$ where $D$ is the quarter disk $x^{2}+y^{2}\le 16,$ $x,y\ge 0.$ So $M_{xy}=\frac{1}{2}M_{yz}$ (both are finite: $\iint_{D}x^{2}\,dA=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\int_{0}^{4}r^{3}\cos^{2}\theta\,dr\,d\theta=16\pi$).

Consider the solid enclosed by the cylinder $x^{2}+z^{2}=a^{2}$ and the planes $y=b$ and $y=c,$ where $a\gt 0$ and $b\lt c$ are real numbers. The density of $Q$ is given by $\rho (x,y,z)=f'(y),$ where $f$ is a differential function whose derivative is continuous on $(b,c).$ Show that if $f(b)=f(c),$ then the moment of inertia about the $xz\text{-plane}$ of $Q$ is null.

answer.solution: The moment of inertia about the $xz$-plane is $I_{y}=\iiint_{Q}(x^{2}+z^{2})\rho\,dV.$ The solid is the disk $x^{2}+z^{2}\le a^{2}$ swept from $y=b$ to $y=c,$ and $\rho=f^{\prime}(y)$ depends on $y$ only, so $I_{y}=\int_{b}^{c}f^{\prime}(y)\,dy\cdot\iint_{x^{2}+z^{2}\le a^{2}}(x^{2}+z^{2})\,dA=[f(c)-f(b)]\cdot\frac{\pi a^{4}}{2}.$ If $f(b)=f(c),$ the first factor is $0,$ so $I_{y}=0.$

Show that the moments of inertia $I_{x},I_{y},\text{and}\;I_{z}$ about the $yz\text{-plane,}$ $xz\text{-plane,}$ and $xy\text{-plane,}$ respectively, of the unit ball centered at the origin whose density is $\rho (x,y,z)=e^{-x^{2}-y^{2}-z^{2}}$ are the same. Round your answer to two decimal places.

For the following problems, find the center of mass of the region.

$\rho (x,y)=xy$ on the circle with radius $1$ in the first quadrant only.

For the following problems, find the center of mass of the region.

$\rho (x,y,z)=z$ on the inverted cone with radius $2$ and height $2.$

The following problems concern the Theorem of Pappus (see Moments and Centers of Mass for a refresher), a method for calculating volume using centroids. Assuming a region $R,$ when you revolve around the $x\text{-axis}$ the volume is given by $V_{x}=2\pi A\overline{|y|},$ and when you revolve around the $\text{y-axis}$ the volume is given by $V_{y}=2\pi A|\bar{x}|,$ where $A$ is the area of $R.$ Consider the region bounded by $x^{2}+y^{2}=1$ and above $y=x+1.$

Find the volume when you revolve the region around the $x\text{-axis.}$
